text:
MEASURED 2026-08-03, before starting the migration. This bead asked for a before/after benchmark so the claimed win would be measured rather than asserted. Running that measurement first refutes the stated mechanism and redirects the work.

REFUTED: "FrameDecoder.feed is quadratic because it accumulates with buffered ++ input on every chunk."
Sweeping payload 512 KiB -> 4 MiB in 64 KiB chunks (9 -> 65 chunks), fastest of 10 after 5 warmups:
  512 KiB,  9 chunks, 0.11 ms
 1024 KiB, 17 chunks, 0.12 ms
 2048 KiB, 33 chunks, 0.07 ms
 4096 KiB, 65 chunks, 0.12 ms
Time is FLAT across an 8x payload increase and a 7x chunk-count increase. Not quadratic, not even linear in bytes. The reason: Scala 3 Vector is a radix-balanced trie, so ++, take and drop copy spine nodes only and never touch the payload. Related common assumption, also false: boxing a Byte never allocates, because java.lang.Byte.valueOf caches all 256 values. There is no win available at FrameCodec.scala:40, so it must come off the hot-path list rather than stay as a headline.

CONFIRMED: the ~5x memory claim. A 4 MiB payload retains 18.9 MiB as Vector[Byte], about 4.7x the data, consistent with one reference per element plus trie node overhead. (The harness measured Array[Byte] at 8.0 MiB against a true 4 MiB, so treat the absolute array figure as noise and the Vector figure as the meaningful one.)

FOUND, and this is the actual cost: unboxing at every array boundary. Vector[Byte].toArray over 4 MiB takes 2.76 ms (1451 MiB/s) against 0.45 ms for Array.clone (8898 MiB/s), so 6x slower. Every base64 encode and decode, every content digest, every ByteBuffer write and every FS2 Chunk conversion pays it, once per payload. For scale: that single conversion costs 23x the entire 4 MiB frame decode this bead singled out. Attention was pointed at the wrong place by more than an order of magnitude.

ByteVector addresses both real costs: it is backed by byte arrays, so toArray is a bulk System.arraycopy near the 0.45 ms figure, and its footprint is the data size.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD. The plan and the module order are unchanged and still correct; the justification and the evidence criteria are not.
- Replace the "recorded before/after benchmark of FrameDecoder.feed" criterion. It cannot show a win because there is none there. Measure instead the array-conversion boundary and the retained footprint, which is where the benefit is.
- Remove FrameCodec / FrameDecoder.feed from "hot paths where the benefit must actually be shown". Keep CommonLogRecognizer.recognize, which is a different mechanism (a full boxed lowercase copy plus eight naive searches over O(log n) random access) and is still worth measuring on its own.
- The byte-identical-fixture safety argument is untouched and remains the basis for doing this safely.
- The sequencing rationale is also untouched: this still blocks P6f.12, and doing the representation change before hand-writing every codec still avoids writing them twice. That, not throughput, is now the primary reason to do this bead.

Harnesses committed under modules/protocol/src/test as FrameDecoderBenchmark and ByteRepresentationBenchmark so the after-numbers are produced the same way.
